title: Two debts: does the order matter?
hook: Same $300 a month, same two debts. Could the order you pay them in change the bill?

knows: that card debt is charged interest each month
doesNotKnow: that the order of repayment changes the total interest paid

misconception: The order I pay debts in makes no difference to the cost.
objective: The learner can explain that money which clears a higher-rate balance first stops more interest being added: with $300 a month, paying the 24% debt first costs about $300 less than paying the $1,000 6% debt first.

claims.text: Paying the $4,000 24% debt first (then the $1,000 6% debt) with $300 a month costs $793 of interest and is done in 20 months.
claims.source: Monthly: add each balance × APR/12, then pay $300 to the 24% debt first, any leftover that month to the other. Total 793.19, 20 months. Deterministic. Demo.tsx run('high').

claims.text: Paying the $1,000 6% debt first costs $1,095 of interest and is done in 21 months.
claims.source: Same stepping with the 6% debt first: total 1,094.57, 21 months. Demo.tsx run('low').
From the rounded totals the stage shows: 1,095 − 793 = 302. Exact difference 1,094.57 − 793.19 = 301.37.

claims.text: Each month the 24% balance adds 2% of itself and the 6% balance 0.5%, so a dollar that clears the 24% debt stops four times as much interest.
The lesson is a model: fixed rates charged monthly (APR / 12), no minimum payments, no new spending; it is arithmetic about this model, not advice to anyone.
claims.source: Assumptions of Demo.tsx; stage chip 'Model: fixed rates, no minimums, no new spending'. Real cards may compound daily and require minimums on every debt.

recall.question: Two debts, one at 5% and one at 20%. A fixed amount a month goes to one at a time. Which order adds less interest?
recall.why: The higher-rate balance adds more interest per dollar each month, so clearing it first stops the most interest from being added.
